title: Analytica explicatio methodi maximorum et minimorum

deep.reconstruction:
§XXIX is a worked example of the general theory in §§XXVI–XXVIII. Euler minimises J = ∫ √(1+p²)/√y dx, with p = dy/dx, up to x = a. This is the brachistochrone functional, with y measured downward. The value of y at x = a is left free.

Here Z = √(1+p²)/√y, so M = 0, N = −√(1+p²)/(2y√y) and P = p/(√y√(1+p²)). The Euler–Lagrange equation is N − dP/dx = 0. Because M = 0 he multiplies by p: N dy = p dP. Since dZ = N dy + P dp = p dP + P dp, integration gives the first integral Z − pP = C (the Beltrami/energy integral). This becomes 1/(√y √(1+p²)) = 1/√b, i.e. y(1+p²) = b. Then dx = y dy/√(by − y²), and integration gives a cycloid.

The free-end condition from the previously neglected boundary term P δy (§XXVIII) is P = 0 at x = a. That means p = 0, hence y = b: the cycloid reaches the vertical line x = a with a horizontal tangent, at its lowest point. Euler fixes c from this and then imposes y = 0 at x = 0.

§§XXX–XXXI make the method explicit. There are two states, 'principal' and 'varied'. The ordinary differential d moves from x to x+dx within one state. The variation δ moves from the principal to the varied state at fixed x, so δx = 0. The total change of y is dy + δy. For V(x, y, p, q, r, …) with dV = M dx + N dy + P dp + Q dq + …, the variation is δV = M δx + N δy + P δp + Q δq + …. This is the δ-calculus of Lagrange, which Euler adopts and expounds in E296/E297. The next page states the commutation δd = dδ and δ∫ = ∫δ, and the iterated integration-by-parts formulas.
errors: The integration as transcribed, x = c − √(by−yy) + b·A sin(2√(by−yy)/b), has the wrong coefficient. Since ∫ y dy/√(by−y²) = −√(by−y²) + (b/2)·θ with sin θ = 2√(by−y²)/b (the cycloid y = (b/2)(1−cos θ), x = c + (b/2)(θ − sin θ)), the arc term should carry b/2. Consequently c = a − πb/2, not a − πb. With y(0) = 0 one gets b = 2a/π, not a/π. Unless the print has ½b where the transcription and scan read b, Euler's constants are off by a factor 2.
Minor: the multivaluedness of arcsin(2√(by−y²)/b) is not discussed. The arc must pass π/2 at y = b/2 and reach π at y = b.
Euler says 'maximum or minimum'; for this functional (time of descent) it is a minimum. This is routine phrasing.

ideas.what: First integral Z − pP = const when Z does not depend explicitly on x (M = 0)
Free-endpoint condition P = 0 at x = a, from the boundary term P δy; brachistochrone to a vertical line ends with a horizontal tangent
ideas.usually_credited_to: Lagrange (1760–62) and Euler (E296/E297); free-end brachistochrone problems go back to the Bernoullis

ideas.what: Distinction between d (along the curve) and δ (between curves at fixed x, δx = 0), with δV computed by the ordinary differentiation rule
ideas.usually_credited_to: Lagrange (1755 letter to Euler, 1762 paper); Euler's systematization in E296 'Elementa calculi variationum'

deep.surprise_reason: The page holds a standard textbook example (free-end brachistochrone with a natural boundary condition) and an exposition of Lagrange's δ-formalism. Both are well documented in histories of the calculus of variations (e.g. Goldstine, Fraser). The only notable point is an apparent factor-2 slip in the integrated cycloid (b instead of b/2), with the knock-on b = a/π instead of 2a/π. That is an erratum, not a missed result.
transcription_corrections: Section heading appears as 'XX:X.' in the scan but is XXIX.
The arc term in the integrated equation should be checked against the print: it may read ½bA sin. rather than bA sin. (mathematically b/2 is required).
'nanciscimur' is split across lines as 'nancisci-mur' in the original; 'sicque' is spelled 'ficque' with a long s.
